title.narrative: BBSEA Moldova WATERWISE (Wetlands and Terrestrial Ecosystem Restoration for Watershed Improvements and Sustainable Environments)

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.
To increase the area under sustainable landscape management practices within the Dniester River Basin in Moldova

Yes. Please see project document, SEP, GAP, and ESRS for further details. The PAD includes a section on cost-benefit and economic analysis for the project, summarized below:The proposed project’s technical design seeks to improve the ecosystem resilience in the Dniester River Basin. Forest floor litter captures particles and chemicals, preventing them from entering water bodies. Organic matter in forest soils can also adsorb and degrade pollutants, including nitrogen and phosphorus, which are common contributors to water pollution in the Dniester River Basin. Usually, forest vegetation stabilizes soil with its root systems, reducing soil erosion and sedimentation in water bodies. The project will adopt an NBS approach to tackle these pollution and erosion issues and strengthen ecosystem functions, through NBS investments, policy and institutional strengthening and community-based planning and demonstration projects support. The NBS approach adopted by the project will support the reduction of erosion and runoff risks in the targeted watersheds as it increases the services provided by forests to act as natural filters by trapping sediments, nutrients, and pollutants from erosion and runoff. This will also minimize socioeconomic and physical damage exacerbated by climate change through: (i) forest rehabilitation, reforestation and afforestation; (ii) reinvigorate biodiversity by reconstructing and restoring ecosystem functions and adopting substitution of species where needed; and (iii) managing river flows by considering torrent protection shelterbelts, enhanced vegetation buffers and riverbank management and disturbance control. The project will target several public tiers and beneficiaries by building capacity, providing policy support and using adaptive forest management techniques. It will also support citizen engagement through silvopastoral management planning and demonstration projects. The project preparation prioritized areas in the targeted Dniester River Basin after deriving exposure and vulnerability to pollution from runoffs and erosion. It is expected that the NBS approach will effectively regulate the natural flow and improve the water quality in the watersheds, the restoration or conservation of wetlands which have been degraded through uncontrolled upstream land use. The project will also promote sustainable land use and planning (10,000 ha) where demonstration activities and riverbed and wetland protection are considered with the communities over a 200-ha area and restore ecosystem provisioning, regulating, habitat and cultural services that will benefit vulnerable farmers, women and youth living in the targeted watersheds.As the project will improve the watershed ecosystem services owned by the public sector (2,800 ha of which 200 ha are managed by private farmers) that is considered a public good, only an economic analysis based on an ex-ante Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) was performed. Local communities are expected to reap environmental and social benefits of NBS interventions as they will be trained and granted ownership over their implementation and outcomes. This analysis focuses on a subset of anticipated project benefits that can be quantified and selects conservative estimates for all indicators. All quantifiable and tangible benefits are expected to arise from sub-component 2.2. The economic benefits from the project are expected to contribute more to restoring critical ecosystem services (ES) in the Dniester River Basin through NBS approaches. These ES include reduced damage from erosion, nutrient pollution, flooding, improved livelihoods (e.g., increased agricultural productivity), and other goods and services provided through ecosystem restoration. The proposed project will help access more ecosystem benefits by expanding areas of healthier ecosystems (restored functionality) improving landscape/habitat conditions and water quality at the upstream and downstream watersheds. Restoration (forest and wetland) and conservation (sustainable forest management) activities with NBS will involve catchment/watershed management measures on nearly 2,000 ha upstream. It will directly capture regulatory ES by reducing soil erosion, water purification, restoration of natural habitats and improving biodiversity, reducing risks of floods, ultimately allowing to improve livelihoods of local population downstream. Sub-component 2.2 has a positive Net Present Value (NPV) of US$1.3 million as well as a positive economic IRR of 9 percent and a positive Present Value benefit-cost ratio of 1.2. The sensitivity analysis shows that investment is more sensitive to a reduction in benefits than in costs. The project remains viable with a 4 percent but not with an 8 percent discount rates. Under the optimistic scenario with a 10 percent increase in benefits and a 10 percent reduction in costs, the project generates a NPV of US$4.9 million discounted at 4 percent, an economic IRR of 12 percent and a Present Value Benefit-Cost ratio of 1.9. Under the pessimistic scenario with a 10 percent increase in costs and a 10 percent reduction in benefits, the project generates a negative NPV of US$1.1 million discounted at 8 percent, an economic IRR of 5 percent and a Present Value Benefit-Cost ratio of 0.9. Moreover, a yearly US$ 2.6 million knock-on effect on the local economy will occur after the creation of 300 green jobs by the end of the project.Improvement of provisioning ES will have a significant development impact, improving the life of rural communities, especially the most vulnerable groups and women. It will help address poverty in rural villages, where income is heavily reliant on agriculture and remittances from family members working elsewhere. By improving agricultural productivity, the project is projected to increase incomes of direct beneficiaries. The project will field test innovative and inclusive ecosystem restoration, forest and agroforest/silvopastoral management practices and models that aim to enhance and increase social benefits and community empowerment (related to local responsibilities, benefit sharing and landscape planning), which is expected to build social capital and empower communities and their institutions, including for women. The benefits from restored ES and reduced nutrient pollution could be multiplied with averting climate change impacts considering the estimate of an average loss of US$40 million per year in foregone agricultural production due to soil erosion in Moldova and increasing frequency and intensity of droughts . The improved frameworks for marine pollution management, forest and wetland restorations, and watershed management aligning these with European Union and international obligations including NDC commitments will bring additional benefits in adapting to climate change.----Additional information on Stakeholders, Environmental and Social:The Moldova Project is being prepared under the World Bank’s Environment and Social Framework (ESF). Per Environmental and Social Standard (or hereafter ESS) 10 on Stakeholder Engagement and Information Disclosure, the implementing agencies should provide stakeholders with timely, relevant, understandable, and accessible information, and consult with them in a culturally appropriate manner, which is free of manipulation, interference, coercion, discrimination, or intimidation. The overall objective of the Project Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP) is to define a program for stakeholder engagement, including public information disclosure and consultation throughout the entire project cycle. The SEP outlines the ways in which the PIU will communicate with stakeholders and includes a mechanism by which people can raise concerns, provide feedback, or make complaints about project activities or any activities related to the projectKey stakeholders are being consulted since the concept stage of the proposed project in an inclusive manner, which include local community representatives, NGOs, research institutes and central and local government entities responsible for environment, forest, water resource management. Their input has informed the project design, which includes the type of intervention, site selection, identification of potential E&S risks and impacts and their mitigations and implementation arrangements. From September 2 to 13, the client, together with the Bank team, met with representatives of Moldsilva (both headquarter and local units), AAM, districts and villages within the Dniester River Basin (in the north, central and southern Moldova), NGOs (Biotica, Arboretum.md, 100 Frontiers), and ICAS. During its preparatory phase the project concept has been consulted with a broad variety of key national stakeholders (including the representatives of authorities, subordinated agencies, local public authorities, research/academia, business, and civil society institutions and community representatives).At the same time, during the period of September 2-13, 2024, the implementing agencies and the World Bank team conducted site visits and met with key stakeholders, including Local Public Administration officials (mayors and officers in potential project sites), State Forestry Enterprises, local business representatives (local winery and cement factory), Forest Research and Management Institute (ICAS Chisinau), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), as well as local community members (local forest rangers, farmers, shepherds and other villagers). Stakeholders expressed broader support to the project. Additional project consultations took place on September 30, 2024. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan was updated and disclosed.As part of CHOIP, the project will develop a Private Sector Engagement Strategy (PSES) to ensure collaboration with key private sector entities, such as fertilizer companies, agri-food businesses, water supply firms, tourism businesses, fishing companies, the banking industry etc. This process involves a detailed process for stakeholder mapping, characterization, categorization, leading to a comprehensive plan with specific engagement mechanisms and activities per key private sector groups that will be identified. The project will work with the GCP to ensure a harmonized approach to implementing the SEP and the PSES. The project will use is own financial support from the IA to develop and implement these plans but may require additional technical support from the CGP, which would require additional financial contribution form the project budget.The proposed project has been assessed with moderate environmental risks but is expected to have a positive long-term impact. None of its activities are likely to cause biodiversity loss or environmental damage. The project's social risks are considered moderate. It involves small-scale physical works to restore 2,700 ha of degraded forest and wetland sites along the Dniester River and improve agroforestry and silvopastoral practices across 10,000 ha (including at least 100 ha of demo sites).The project will generate significantly positive environmental effects on the watershed level, with various measures intended upstream in order to reduce marine pollution carried downstream by the Dniester River. No significant environmental risks are expected neither at the construction or operation stages of the project. The envisaged environmental and social risks are considered moderate, which are related to minor civil works for wetland restoration, rehabilitation of small rivers beds and afforestation/ reforestation activities. While the proposed project will take the NBS approach, no significant civil works are anticipated. The areas of intervention will not interfere with special conservation zones as the Ramsar sites. Mitigation measures will be implemented to address environmental risks associated with small civil works as described above. Social risks are also considered moderate. Project interventions are expected to take place on public land (state or community) and no land acquisition and physical and economic resettlement are anticipated. Any involuntary restrictions to land use or natural resources (for example, site-specific temporary access restrictions at reforestation sites or civil work site) will be appropriately avoided, minimized and managed through close engagement with key stakeholders. Labor and working conditions and OHS and community health and safety risks will be managed through appropriate mitigation and monitoring measures, including appropriate use of PPE (such as for forest/wetland restoration activities and silvopastoral planning). Social tensions and exclusion risks may arise from site or beneficiaries’ selection processes, if the criteria are not sufficiently consulted and disseminated with a wide range of stakeholders and beneficiaries in local areas, including those who are more likely to be poor, women and youth who are considered disadvantaged in terms of engagement and access to economic opportunities in the agricultural sector. To address such risks, the project design includes activities to strengthen community capacity for conservation and offer opportunities for stakeholder engagement and employment. The PIU will prepare appropriate E&S instruments, which will guide risk screening and application of mitigation measures at the sub-project level under the project. Once the areas of intervention are identified, a thorough screening of potential risks will be undertaken, and relevant mitigation measures will be put in place and monitored for all project interventions.
